title: Terms
text: One key + passphrase · Step 1 of 12 Terms ← Home Step 1 of 12 · Terms 2 · Before you begin → Time 10 min Difficulty Easy Steps 12 terms You will need: Nothing, just read The words you need before the work begins. Use these definitions as a reference throughout the guide. No secrets are needed to search. Find a term 12 terms shown. Seed phrase A human-readable backup used to derive wallet keys. Keep it secret. Recovery may also require a passphrase and, for multisig, the wallet configuration. Passphrase An additional secret used with a BIP39 seed phrase to derive a different wallet. The exact value matters: a typo can open a different, empty wallet. It is not the device PIN. Entropy Unpredictable input used to generate keys. Correct dice collection can provide entropy; it does not protect against malicious software that handles the result. BIP39 A specification for encoding entropy and a checksum as a mnemonic and deriving a seed from it, with an optional passphrase. It is more than a word list. Airgap Separation from networks. In this guide, secret-handling sessions use verified offline software. Turning networking off does not prove the computer is free of malware. Hash · file fingerprint A digest used to detect file changes. A match is useful only if the expected value comes from a trustworthy source; an attacker can replace both a file and its published hash. Digital signature A cryptographic check that a file was signed by a particular key and has not changed. Verify the signer’s key fingerprint independently; “Good signature” alone does not identify a trustworthy author. Extended public key · xpub Public information that can derive a branch of wallet addresses. It does not authorize spending on its own, but revealing it can expose wallet activity. Wallet descriptor A description of the scripts and public-key information used by a wallet. A watch-only descriptor is not a signing secret, but it is privacy-sensitive and important for multisig recovery. 2-of-3 multisig A wallet policy requiring signatures from two of three keys. Recovering with two seeds also needs the missing cosigner’s public information and the correct policy. PSBT Partially Signed Bitcoin Transaction: a format for carrying transaction details and signatures between wallet software and signers. It can be used with single-signature and multisig wallets. Watch-only wallet A wallet holding public information so it can display addresses and transactions. It cannot sign by itself. Verify its receive addresses against independently trusted wallet details. Independent verification: two matching tools are not enough if both rely on the same compromised input. Check the source of the data as well as the result. Specifications: BIP39 · PSBT (BIP174) . ← Home Step 1 of 12 2 · Before you begin →

title: Before you begin
text: One key + passphrase · Step 2 of 12 Before you begin ← 1 · Terms Step 2 of 12 · Before you begin 3 · Pick your path → Time 5 min Difficulty Easy Steps 1 worksheet You will need: Pen and paper What are you protecting your Bitcoin from? Two quick questions help you identify your risks. No secret keys or personal information are collected. 1 Choose your concerns ✓ Theft Someone gets access to a backup. ✓ Fire or flood A backup location is destroyed. ✓ Mistakes I lose or record something incorrectly. ✓ Scams Someone tricks me into sharing a secret. ✓ Inheritance My family needs to recover my Bitcoin. 2 Where is your Bitcoin today? On an exchange Someone else controls the keys. Phone or software wallet My keys are on an internet-connected device. Hardware wallet I already use a dedicated signing device. I haven't started I want to begin correctly. Your security priorities Select the risks you want to plan for, then choose where your Bitcoin is today. These choices help you think through risks; they do not automatically determine a safe wallet configuration. Choose your path → Explore wallet risks and tradeoffs One key and a passphrase Simpler to operate, but forgetting or losing the passphrase can permanently prevent recovery. A compromised device or poorly stored backup can still put funds at risk. Keep the passphrase on paper apart from the plate. If someone finds both the seed backup and its passphrase, they may be able to access your funds. Keep them separately and test restoration. One device, one maker. A flawed or tampered device can still fail you. Words and passphrase go into the device itself during recovery, nowhere else. No hardware company will ever ask for your seed phrase. Check the receiving address on the device screen, not only on the computer screen, before you accept coins. The watch-only wallet cannot sign. Spending requires the signing key for the passphrase-protected wallet; recovery requires the seed and the exact passphrase. A replacement compatible device can be used. Three keys (2-of-3 multisig) Separates signing keys across devices or locations, but makes setup and recovery more complicated. Securely preserve the wallet configuration/descriptor and test the recovery procedure. Most steps to get right. A missed step in any key can lock the wallet later. If fewer than two signing keys remain available, you cannot spend, even with the wallet map. Losing the map can also prevent recovery when the missing public-key information cannot be reconstructed. Keep three plates in three places, and keep the encrypted map apart from any single plate. Two signing keys meet the 2-of-3 threshold, but recovery also requires the correct wallet configuration. Keep verified copies of the descriptor and recovery instructions in separate safe locations, and rehearse reconstruction and spending before funding the wallet. No passphrase on the 2-of-3. The protection comes from three keys in three places, not from a passphrase. Practice spend first, and rehearse on testnet if you have not done this before. Savings do not move until the practice spend works. Shut down fully between keys. A key left in memory is a key at risk. Note: One stolen seed being insufficient applies to an appropriately configured 2-of-3 multisig, not all wallets. Multisig does not automatically solve scams, user error, coercion, or inheritance. Test recovery before trusting a wallet with meaningful funds. Never type seed phrases or passphrases into a website, form, or demo. ← 1 · Terms Step 2 of 12 3 · Pick your path →

title: Checklist
text: One key + passphrase · Step 4 of 12 Checklist ← 3 · Pick your path Step 4 of 12 · Checklist 5 · Two boots → Prepare the materials and the recovery plan before creating keys. Private workspace Fair dice with readable faces, a fixed reading order, a numbered recording sheet, and a pen. A workspace without cameras, microphones, or observers recording secrets. Time to stop and investigate any mismatch without rushing. Verified offline setup Prepare the Tails USB and a separate transfer USB. Read Two boots and Check the files before using downloads. Transfer media must never carry signing secrets back online. The kit contains version-pinned instructions. Confirm that each release, signature and hash belong together; do not substitute a newer binary while keeping an old manifest. Compatibility and version reconciliation remain under review. Backup materials Plan a durable backup for the one seed and a separate secure record of the exact passphrase. Keep these apart from each other and from the signing device. Choose a backup format you can read and test. Product capacity varies; this guide does not require a particular brand or forbid additional secured copies. Recovery records Record the wallet software, network, script type, account and derivation path. Preserve a verified public descriptor if your wallet supports exporting one. Prepare a private location record and instructions a trusted helper can understand. Rehearse with a disposable test wallet before relying on the process for savings. Before proceeding: review how you will recover the seed backup and the exact wallet passphrase. Having the equipment is not proof that the wallet is recoverable. ← 3 · Pick your path Step 4 of 12 5 · Two boots →

title: Two boots
text: One key + passphrase · Step 5 of 12 Two boots ← 4 · Checklist Step 5 of 12 · Two boots 6 · Check the files → Time 45 min Difficulty Careful Steps 4 sections You will need: Everyday computer · Tails USB Separate online preparation from offline secret handling. This page explains the session boundaries. Read Check the files and complete verification before installing or running downloaded software. Page order is not permission to skip that check. Limits: Tails and Offline Mode cannot make compromised hardware or firmware trustworthy. Reusing one computer for several keys creates shared risks that a reboot does not remove. Online preparation Download and verify first Follow the official Tails installation instructions for your computer and release. Authenticate the image before writing it. Keep a separate data USB for the specific verified files you need. Do not put seed phrases, raw entropy, private keys, or passphrases on the data USB or in the everyday operating system. Do not create or unlock Persistent Storage for this guide’s temporary secret-handling sessions. Offline session Set the boundary before secrets At the Tails Welcome Screen, enable Offline Mode before starting the desktop. Older instructions may call this networking disabled. Disconnect network cables and do not enable networking during the session. Use only the verified local tools required for the task. A webpage’s “offline” badge is a reminder, not proof of network isolation or a safe computer. One key or three? The one-key path creates one seed. The three-key path uses a separate session for each seed. Do not load multiple signing seeds in one session. Separate sessions reduce accidental mixing; they do not establish independent hardware trust. Transfer boundary Export only what the next step needs When the guide calls for a transfer, export only reviewed public wallet information or the required transaction file. Public descriptors and xpubs expose wallet activity and still need privacy protection. Never copy seeds, raw entropy, private-key exports, or secret-bearing wallet files back to the online computer. Do not assume a file is public because its name says “backup.” Inspect the export type and follow the wallet’s documentation. End the session Power off fully Finish the offline task and shut down Tails completely before another key session. Do not substitute suspend or hibernate. Keep your physical backup private, away from cameras and microphones. Shutdown ends the session; it does not undo a disclosure, erase a file you saved elsewhere, or remove malicious firmware. If isolation or software integrity is in doubt, stop and investigate before using that key. Stop if: verification is incomplete, networking was enabled while a secret was present, a secret was saved to transfer media, or you cannot identify what an export contains. Do not use a real funded wallet for a rehearsal. Official references: Welcome Screen and Offline Mode · Untrusted computer risks . Next, Check the files. Return to these session rules when the later steps require offline work. ← 4 · Checklist Step 5 of 12 6 · Check the files →

title: Check the files
text: One key + passphrase · Step 6 of 12 Check the files ← 5 · Two boots Step 6 of 12 · Check the files 7 · Make one key → Time 30 min Difficulty Careful Steps 7 sections You will need: The downloaded files · Two verification tools Verify the file, its source, and the signing key before running it. Staging guide: a familiar domain or HTTPS connection does not certify software safety. This site’s tools and instructions remain under review. Never enter signing secrets into the live website. 1 · Source Start with the project Use the developer’s official download and verification instructions for the exact release and operating system. Avoid links from advertisements, unsolicited messages, or search-result lookalikes. For this kit, the downloads page and manifest identify distributed files. They do not independently audit their code. What HTTPS tells you HTTPS protects the connection to the named domain. It does not prove that the domain, its publisher, or the downloaded program is trustworthy. 2 · Integrity Compare the complete hash Calculate the downloaded file’s SHA-256 digest and compare every character with the authenticated expected value for that exact release. The file checker can compare a kit file with its listed digest. A match means the bytes agree with the reference. If an attacker replaces both the file and the reference, that comparison will still pass. Command-line alternatives On macOS, use shasum -a 256 followed by the file path. In Windows PowerShell, use Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 with the file path. Follow the project’s instructions for your platform. 3 · Authenticity Verify the signer, then the signature Where the publisher provides signatures, authenticate the signing key’s full fingerprint using the publisher’s documented verification process and an independently trusted source. Then verify the signature for the exact downloaded file or signed checksum manifest. “Good signature” alone is insufficient. It means the signature verifies under a key; you must establish whose key it is. A new key or unexplained fingerprint change needs investigation. About trust warnings A message that a key is not certified can reflect your local trust settings. Do not dismiss it without independently checking the key identity. Stop for a bad signature, unexpected key, or unresolved warning. 4 · Ready to proceed? Keep a verification record Record the release, file name, hash, verification method, and signing-key fingerprint when applicable. Run any kit verification script only after reviewing and authenticating that script too. Never run a failed or unexplained download. Recheck the source and release before trying again. A successful checksum or signature does not establish that software is bug-free or appropriate for custody. Stop if: the source is uncertain, a hash differs, a signature fails, the key identity is unverified, or the release cannot be matched to its verification instructions. Do not proceed to secret-handling work. Use the current official instructions: Tails installation · Sparrow downloads and verification . Next, follow your path’s key-generation page. Verify every required file before opening an offline secret-handling session. ← 5 · Two boots Step 6 of 12 7 · Make one key →

title: Make one key
text: One key + passphrase · Step 7 of 12 Make one key ← 6 · Check the files Step 7 of 12 · Make one key 8 · Back up your key → Time 30-45 min Difficulty Moderate Steps 6 sections You will need: 5 dice · Paper and pen · The worksheet You will roll dice to create one Bitcoin seed phrase. Each one becomes 24 words. The computer never sees the network while you work. Safety first: Never enter seed words on an online computer. Boot Tails with networking Disabled before you start. Shut down fully between each key. What you will do Boot Tails offline. Copy the dice converter page. Roll dice. Enter the faces. The page counts to 256 bits. Write down the 24 words. Prove them with a second tool. Shut down after checking the one seed. Do not create additional seeds for this path. Step 1 / 6 Boot Tails. Copy the converter. Boot Tails with networking set to Disabled. Copy the checked dice converter page from the data USB to the Desktop. Check: Open only the verified local copy after enabling Tails Offline Mode. An offline indicator alone does not prove network isolation. If it reports online, stop. Step 2 / 6 Roll the dice. Enter the faces. Roll five dice at once. Enter each face as you roll it. Using fair, independently rolled dice and a fixed reading order, faces 1 to 4 count as bits (1=00, 2=01, 3=10, 4=11). Faces 5 and 6 are skipped, roll those dice again. The page counts the pairs and stops you at 128. SHAKE 1 SHAKE 2 SHAKE 3 11 RE-ROLL 01 00 10 01 01 RE-ROLL 11 11 00 10 00 10 RE-ROLL 00 01 RE-ROLL 10 256-BIT STRING 11 00 10 01 01 01 11 00 10 11 00 10 00 01 10 …keep rolling… 256 / 256 BITS 10 / 256 20 / 256 30 / 256 256 / 256 24 WORDS Roll as many times as needed to get 256 bits of entropy: about 39 shakes. Check: The page shows 128 pairs and 256 bits. Count accepted pairs, not an estimated number of shakes. Step 3 / 6 Write the 24 words. At 256 bits the page prints 24 words. In a 24-word BIP39 phrase, the last word contains three entropy bits and eight checksum bits. It is not an arbitrary check word: never invent or alter it. Write all 24 on the grid. Compare them privately in order, away from cameras and microphones. Check: All 24 words and their positions are recorded accurately; a valid checksum does not prove safe randomness. Step 4 / 6 Prove it with a second tool. Use a separately verified offline implementation with the exact same 256-bit entropy and BIP39 settings. Raw dice inputs are not interchangeable between tools: some hash the roll string while this guide maps accepted faces to bit pairs. Confirm the input method before comparing all 24 words. If you cannot establish that the inputs and method match, stop; do not guess or choose a preferred output. Check: Both tools show the same 24 words. Step 5 / 6 Finish the one-key session. Finish checking the one seed, then shut Tails down fully. Keep its backup private. This path does not require a second or third signing seed. Check: One seed is recorded on one numbered grid. No additional signing seeds are needed. Step 6 / 6 Confirm the checks agree. The checksum detects many transcription errors, but not all of them. It does not authenticate the source of the words. At least two checks must agree: the two tools showing the same words, and the wallet (Sparrow or Electrum, offline) opening the list without error. If anything disagrees, stop. Stop if: The page says online. The two tools show different words. The wallet rejects the list. Any of these means stop and start that key over. Next, back up your key using the next page on this path. ← 6 · Check the files Step 7 of 12 8 · Back up your key →

title: Back up your key
text: One key + passphrase · Step 8 of 12 Stamp the plate ← 7 · Make one key Step 8 of 12 · Back up your key 9 · If I am gone → Make a durable backup without losing the ability to recover. Record accurately Back up the one seed using the chosen medium’s instructions. Preserve word order and any required encoding information. Work privately and compare every entry against the original. Keep the original protected while checking the replacement. A damaged or ambiguous mark needs correction before you rely on it. Check recovery safely Use the wallet’s documented backup-check or recovery procedure on trusted equipment. Do not wipe your only working signer to test an unproven backup. Never type seeds into this website or an online form. For a rehearsal, use a disposable test wallet. For an existing funded wallet, plan the verification carefully before changing devices or backups. Keep the complete recovery information Record the wallet software, network, script type, account and derivation path. Preserve a verified public descriptor if your wallet supports exporting one. The exact passphrase is a separate recovery secret, not a device PIN. A different passphrase selects a different wallet. Store a durable, accurate record separately from the seed backup. Plan copies and locations Balance loss, theft, access, and disaster risks. More copies can improve availability and also expose secrets in more places. Document which locations contain which material; do not combine enough signing secrets in one place to defeat your separation plan. Do not destroy an original merely because a new backup looks correct. Retire it only after a successful recovery check and a deliberate review of the remaining copies. Revisit the plan when locations or helpers change. Stop if: a backup is unreadable, the recovered wallet differs, or any required passphrase or configuration is missing. Do not overwrite or discard the remaining working material. ← 7 · Make one key Step 8 of 12 9 · If I am gone →

title: If I am gone
text: One key + passphrase · Step 9 of 12 If I am gone Choose a path One device One key + passphrase Three keys ← 8 · Back up your key Step 9 of 12 · If I am gone 10 · If you get stuck → Help a trusted person understand what to find—and when to stop. Leave a clear private plan Describe the wallet type, the location of the full instructions, the required recovery items, and a trusted contact who can explain the process. Keep signing secrets out of this website, email, and the general instruction sheet. Separate ownership and access arrangements from the technical recovery instructions. Make sure the intended person can find the plan when needed. Identify the required items This path requires the seed backup and the exact wallet passphrase. Record the wallet software, network, script type, account and derivation path. Preserve a verified public descriptor if your wallet supports exporting one. The passphrase cannot be reset by a wallet company. A wallet opened without it, or with a typo, may show a different balance. Do not assume that balance represents all of the owner’s funds. Confirm the recovered wallet Follow the recorded, rehearsed procedure and verify the policy and wallet details against independent trusted records. An address match alone does not establish that a coordinator is trustworthy. If the wallet is empty or differs from the records, stop. Check the passphrase, account, network, derivation information and synchronization before concluding funds are lost. Do not overwrite backups or create replacement keys as a guess. Practice before an emergency Walk through locating the records and explaining the steps with the intended helper. Use a disposable test wallet for hands-on training, without exposing the owner’s signing secrets. When a legitimate recovery is needed, independently verify the destination and transaction details on trusted signing equipment. A small successful transfer is useful evidence, but it is not a complete audit of the recovery setup. Protect the secrets: no legitimate support agent needs a seed phrase or private key. If the instructions, equipment compatibility, or wallet identity are uncertain, stop before entering secrets or signing. ← 8 · Back up your key Step 9 of 12 10 · If you get stuck →

title: If you get stuck
text: One key + passphrase · Step 10 of 12 If you get stuck ← 9 · If I am gone Step 10 of 12 · If you get stuck 11 · Recovery card → Time 10 min Difficulty Easy Steps 7 questions You will need Nothing, find your question Find the question that matches your problem. When in doubt, stop is always a valid step. What am I actually making? One key plus a passphrase. The 24 words go on a device, the passphrase goes on paper apart from the plate, and a watch-only wallet watches the coins. The device and the passphrase together can spend. I already own a hardware wallet. Do I start there? Stamp the words in titanium first. Then enter the words and the passphrase on the device itself, never on a computer, phone, or website. Keep the passphrase paper apart from the plate at all times. The download is newer than the version on the sheet. Stop. This kit checks Tails 7.13, Sparrow 2.5.5, Electrum 4.8.2. A newer file will not match. That is a stop, not an upgrade. Delete it. The two word lists don’t match. Stop. Don’t pick the nicer list. Don’t “fix” word 24. Roll again or find the copying mistake. A fixed word is a destroyed key. Can I keep the words in a password manager? No. A photo, note, password manager, or email is one hacked account from the whole seed. Words go on metal, passphrase goes on paper. Never together, never in a password manager. If the plate and the passphrase paper are found together, the passphrase adds nothing. What if the passphrase is lost? The wallet is gone, even with the plate and the device in hand. There is no way back without it. Back up the passphrase paper in a second place, apart from the plate, before you fund the wallet. What does my family do? Leave a written note, apart from both the plate and the passphrase paper, saying where the device is, where the plate is, and where the passphrase paper is, and that all three are needed together. Do not write the passphrase itself in the note. Do not send them the multisig inheritance sheet. It does not match this wallet. ← 9 · If I am gone Step 10 of 12 11 · Recovery card →

title: Recovery card
text: One key + passphrase · Step 11 of 12 Recovery card ← 10 · If you get stuck Step 11 of 12 · Recovery card 12 · One key + passphrase → A private pointer to your recovery plan—not a wallet backup. What this card is for A short location record helps an authorized person find the complete instructions and required materials. It cannot replace the seed backup and the exact wallet passphrase. Location information can help a thief too. Protect the card even though it contains no signing secrets. Write these pointers offline Wallet type: one key + passphrase. Where to find the complete recovery instructions. Seed-backup location and separate passphrase-record location. Trusted contact and date last reviewed. Location of any separate decryption instructions, if required. Write privately on paper. This page intentionally provides no form for entering real locations or secrets. Never include these No seed words, raw entropy, private keys, wallet passphrases, or decryption passwords on the card. Keep it separate from the materials it points to. A descriptor can contain private keys; only a verified public-only export belongs in the non-signing configuration records. Keep it current Check that the intended person can follow the pointers. Update the record after moving a backup or changing the recovery plan, then account for obsolete copies. The downloadable legacy card/PDF has not yet been reconciled with these revised instructions. Do not treat that older packet as a verified version of this page. Recovery still requires verification: use the complete, rehearsed procedure. A list of locations, a device brand, or a derivation-path label is not sufficient by itself. ← 10 · If you get stuck Step 11 of 12 12 · One key + passphrase →

title: One key + passphrase
text: One key + passphrase · Step 12 of 12 One key, done right ← 11 · Recovery card Step 12 of 12 · One key + passphrase Review this path → Time 1-2 hours Difficulty Careful Steps 8 sections You will need: Your hardware wallet · Titanium plates · Pen and paper The seed lives in one device and on one stamped plate. A passphrase guards it, kept on paper in a different place from the plate. This sheet is the whole wallet. Files used: Sparrow 2.5.5 for the watch-only wallet. SEED TOUCHED THE INTERNET Coins in a phone app or on an exchange → PORT OVER · STEP 2 SEED BORN ON THE DEVICE Never typed, photographed, or stored anywhere digital → UPGRADE IN PLACE · STEP 3 The seed phrase is the wallet. The device only signs. One rule: the words go into the device itself, during recovery, and nowhere else. Never a website, never an app, never a form from an email. No hardware company will ever ask for your seed phrase. If a message asks, the message is the attack, no matter how official it looks. Step 1 · Grade your seed. Was the seed made on the device itself, or in an app? Has it ever been typed, photographed, or stored in any digital form (a notes app, a photo, a cloud drive, a password manager)? Do you hold it on paper or metal, in a place only you know? Any wrong answer: the seed counts as exposed. Step 2 is not optional. No seed yet (coins on an exchange): also Step 2. Clean seed (born on the device, never copied anywhere digital): Step 3. A device bought used, or from a marketplace seller, is not a signer. It is a suspect. Buy from the maker's own shop. Step 2 · Exposed seed: port over. 1 · VERIFY Check the files Every tool verified first ↓ 2 · BOOT OFFLINE Tails, networking disabled No Persistent Storage ↓ 3 · ROLL ONE KEY Five dice, faces 1 to 4 Two tools must agree ↓ 4 · RESTORE ON THE DEVICE Every word entered on the device itself Word 24 is a checksum. It is never invented. If the two tools disagree, stop. Write the 24 words on paper, then type them into the device on the device itself,* in its own restore menu, on its own screen. Then shut everything down. No program on a computer does the restore, not Sparrow, and not a text field in a companion app. If a device needs its companion app to start the restore (BitBox App for a BitBox02, Blockstream Green for a Jade), the app only opens the connection. The words still go in on the device, never typed into the computer. The device signs. Boot your trusted online computer for Sparrow. Sparrow meets the device afterward, in Step 6, as the watch-only wallet that builds transactions for the device to sign. The fresh seed has now lived in exactly two places: the offline boot, which forgot it, and the device. Steps 4 and 5 come before any coins move. The old device stays on as the signer, and the old seed retires. * A device adds trust in its maker: the firmware on it, the chip inside it, and the shop it came from. The trade buys something real. A key the everyday computer never holds cannot be stolen by malware on that computer, and the device screen shows every address before you sign. 1 · PAPER 24 words written down Fresh seed from the offline boot ↓ 2 · RESTORE ON THE DEVICE Typed in on its own screen Its own restore menu ↓ 3 · THE DEVICE SIGNS Boot on trusted online computer The 2-of-3 build signs in Tails ↓ 4 · SPARROW, WATCH-ONLY Builds transactions, cannot spend Step 6, after the restore ✕ WORDS NEVER GO INTO A COMPUTER Not Sparrow, not Electrum, no text field Step 3 · Clean seed: upgrade in place. Keep the seed. Nothing about it changes. The work is everything around it: passphrase (Step 4), metal (Step 5), watch-only (Step 6). Go straight to Step 4. Step 4 · Add a passphrase. ROLL 1 OF 6 ROLL 2 OF 6 ROLL 3 OF 6 ROLL 4 OF 6 ROLL 5 OF 6 ROLL 6 OF 6 4 3 4 6 3 4 2 1 2 5 4 5 2 1 2 5 5 1 6 1 1 3 2 2 2 3 3 3 2 3 EFF WORDLIST 43463 panoramic 42125 nectar 45212 precut 55161 smith 13222 banana 33323 handclap 6 WORDS, ABOUT 77 BITS 6 WORDS Fixed example. Roll real dice yourself. Faces 1 to 6 are all kept. No rerolls. Watch how it works: Open the demo full screen A passphrase is one more secret, not a word or short phrase you choose, entered on the device after the seed. Roll five dice, look the number up in the EFF Long Wordlist, write down the word, and repeat to at least six words. On this sheet it is required. One seed in one place is why: a plate found or stolen without the passphrase opens an empty wallet. Forgotten passphrase: the coins are gone, and nobody can reset it. Handed to a scammer along with the words: it stops nothing. Words and passphrase are never kept together and never given to anyone. Write the passphrase on paper. Keep that paper in a different place from the plate. Never write it on the plate. Keep a small spending balance in the wallet without the passphrase. A plate found under pressure has something to show, and it is not your savings. Prove it works: note the first receiving address of the passphrase wallet. The restore check in Step 5 must bring back that same address. If it does not, no real money moves. Step 5 · Stamp it in metal. One seed, one plate, stamped the way teaches. Read the finished plate back, word by word, against the paper. Restore check: wipe the device or use a second one, restore from the plate plus the passphrase, confirm the Step 4 address comes back. Destroy the seed paper only when the restore checks out. The passphrase paper is not destroyed. It lives in its own place, apart from the plate. Step 6 · Watch-only, and the first coins. 1 · WATCH-ONLY BUILDS Sparrow, everyday computer Sees balances, cannot spend ↓ 2 · DEVICE SIGNS The seed never touches that computer ↓ 3 · WATCH-ONLY BROADCASTS The finished payment goes out Build the watch-only wallet in Sparrow from the public key the device exports. It sees balances and builds transactions. It cannot spend. Verify the first receiving address on the device screen before anything is sent to it. If the two screens disagree, stop. From an exchange: withdraw to the verified address. A small amount first if the exchange lets you split it. Confirm it lands. Then withdraw the rest. From an old software wallet: send a small test amount to the verified address. Confirm it lands. Then send the rest. When the old wallet reads zero and the move has confirmed, destroy the old seed paper. It protects nothing now, and a live-looking seed in a drawer only confuses the people who find it later. Know the limits One seed is one point of failure. A fire where the plate sleeps ends this wallet. The passphrase paper surviving somewhere else does not rebuild it. Theft of the plate plus the passphrase paper ends it. A word copied wrong and never restore-checked ends it. This sheet beats an exchange account and it beats a seed in a phone. For the people after you: an heir needs the plate, the passphrase paper, and one plain note that says what they are and which device can restore them. shows how that note should read: plain words, no Bitcoin knowledge assumed, a small test send first. Stop if The device, an app, or a website asks you to type the words into a computer or a phone: stop. That is the scam, wearing the device's clothes. The two dice tools print different words: stop. Do not pick the one you like better. A restored wallet shows a different address than the one you noted: stop. No coins move. Anyone asks for your words or your passphrase, for any reason, in any message: stop. The answer is no, forever. Next. ← 11 · Recovery card Step 12 of 12 Review this path →
